{{short description|Egyptian conservation biologist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=April 2016}}
'''Leela Hazzah''' is an Egyptian conservation biologist who works in Kenya and Tanzania. Hazzah grew up in Egypt, and completed her undergraduate and graduate degrees in the United States. In 2007, Hazzah founded Lion Guardians, which works to protect lions in East Africa along with the indigenous [[Maasai people]].<ref name=CNN1/> In 2014, Hazzah was named one of [[CNN]]'s "Top ten heroes" of 2014.<ref name=CNN1>{{cite web|url=http://www.cnn.com/2014/10/02/world/heroes-reveal/ |title=Anderson Cooper reveals the Top 10 CNN Heroes |publisher=CNN.com |date=April 21, 2015 |accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref>

==Childhood and education==
Hazzah grew up in Egypt. As a child, her family members told her stories of listening to roaring lions from the roof of their house, something that was no longer possible because lions were extinct in Egypt.<ref name=CNN2>{{cite web|url=http://www.cnn.com/2014/07/24/world/cnnheroes-hazzah/ |title=Transforming lion killers into 'Lion Guardians' |publisher=[[CNN]]|date= |accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref> Hazzah states that hearing this story inspired her to pursue lion conservation as a career.<ref name=CNN2/> She earned her bachelor's degree in Biology from [[Denison University]] in [[Granville, Ohio]] in the US, graduating in 2002.<ref name=denison>{{cite web |work=Denison University |url=http://denison.edu/feature/leela-hazzah-02-nominated-as-cnn-hero |title=Leela Hazzah '02 nominated as CNN Hero |publisher=Denison.edu |date=July 24, 2014 |accessdate=April 6, 2016 |archive-date=October 12, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161012040039/https://denison.edu/feature/leela-hazzah-02-nominated-as-cnn-hero |url-status=dead }}</ref> While earning her master's degree in conservation Biology, Hazzah carried out research in Kenya, where she witnessed the difficulties of lion conservation.<ref name=CNN2/> She earned her degree from the [[University of Wisconsin, Madison]], where she went on to earn a [[doctorate]] as well.<ref name=denison/> Her research focused on the reasons behind the then-recent increases in lion killings.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2006/05/060522-lions.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060629080640/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2006/05/060522-lions.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=June 29, 2006 |title=Lion Killings Spur Fears of Regional Extinction in Kenya |work=[[National Geographic (magazine)|National Geographic]]|date=October 28, 2010 |accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref>

==Lion Guardians==
Hazzah lived with the indigenous [[Maasai people|Mbirikani Maasai]] for a year, studying their relationship with lions,<ref name=CNN2/><ref name=smh>{{cite web|url=http://www.smh.com.au/world/how-long-will-the-lions-roar-20130311-2fw1s.html |last=Ham|first=Anthony|title=How long will the lions roar? |publisher=[[Sydney Morning Herald]] |date= March 12, 2013|accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref> while working for the group [[Living with Lions (conservation group)|Living with Lions]].<ref>{{cite web|author=Alex Chadwick |url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=101761344 |title=Protecting African Lions: Hunters Turned Guardians |publisher=NPR |date=March 11, 2009 |accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref> Hazzah lived in the region adjacent to the [[Chyulu Hills|Chyulu Hills National Park]], and participated in the daily life of the Maasai community.<ref name=conbio>{{cite web |url=https://conbio.org/membership/members-spotlight/leela-hazzah |title=Member Spotlight: A conservation biologist turns to social science to protect carnivores in Kenya |publisher=Conbio.org |date=July 2012 |accessdate=April 6, 2016 |archive-date=April 1, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160401112427/http://conbio.org/membership/members-spotlight/leela-hazzah |url-status=dead }}</ref> Killing a lion is a rite of passage for young Maasai men. The Maasai have a complex relationship with lions; the lions kill the Maasai's livestock, yet the Maasai appreciate the lions for their beauty.<ref name=CNN2/><ref name=voices>{{cite web|work=Society for Conservation Biology |url=http://voices.nationalgeographic.com/2015/12/17/proving-the-exception-coexistence-between-human-and-lions-is-possible/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151224142824/http://voices.nationalgeographic.com/2015/12/17/proving-the-exception-coexistence-between-human-and-lions-is-possible/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 24, 2015 |title=Proving the Exception: Coexistence between human and lions is possible|publisher=Voices.nationalgeographic.com |date=December 17, 2015 |accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref> Lions are threatened all over their East African habitat, particularly in [[Amboseli National Park]], where Hazzah did a lot of her work.<ref name=voices/><ref name=smh/> In 2007,<ref name=smh/> Hazzah decided to attempt to persuade and teach the Maasai of the potential benefits of lion conservation,<ref name=CNN2/> and her lessons proved to be popular among the Maasai.<ref name=denison/> The idea that the hunters themselves were best placed to protect the lions originally came from a group of hunters that Hazzah had worked with.<ref name=voices/>

This effort became the non-profit organization Lion Guardians.<ref name=CNN2/> The organization hires Maasai warriors as full-time lion protectors. It also gives them field training, sometimes in addition to teaching them how to read and write. Hazzah stated that she had "never imagined when we first started Lion Guardians that we could transform these killers to the point where they would risk their own lives to stop other people from killing lions."<ref name=CNN2/> The program grew rapidly, going from five lion guardians in 2007 to 40 in 2013.<ref name=smh/> The organization has contributed to reducing human-animal conflict in Kenya and Tanzania,<ref name=denison/> and the lion population in the region is showing many signs of recovery.<ref name=voices/> Hazzah stated that part of her success was due to co-opting the traditional values that the Maasai men associated with killing lions, and turning them towards protecting the lions instead.<ref name=smh/> The organization is a part of the network "Living with Lions."<ref name="Audubon">{{cite web|last=Leibach |first=Julie |url=https://www.audubon.org/news/open-source-wildlife-conservation-tracking-lions-and-cows |title=Open Source Wildlife Conservation: Tracking Lions (and Cows) |publisher=Audubon |date=January 31, 2011|accessdate=April 6, 2016}}</ref> In addition to tracking and monitoring lion populations, it also tracks herds of cattle, which often fall prey to lions, which are then killed by the herders.<ref name="Audubon"/>

==Awards and recognitions==
In 2014, Hazzah was named one of [[CNN]]'s "Top ten heroes" of the year.<ref name=CNN1/> She was awarded the "Young Women Conservation Biology Award" from the [[Society for Conservation Biology]], and has also received several other awards and fellowships.<ref name=denison/>
